claims.text: Sustained creep loading in high-entropy-alloy multilayers progressively triggers localized plastic deformation.
Nanoscale multilayer interfaces amplify local stress concentrations under sustained loading.
Multilayer interfaces exhibit heterogeneous short-range chemical order.
Local lattice distortion produces heterogeneous strain or stress fields.
Amplified interfacial stresses enhance dislocation nucleation and motion.
Limited nanotwinning can further accommodate deformation at heterogeneous interfaces.
The combined dislocation and twinning mechanisms can couple substantial plastic deformation with retained strength.
The starting coating consists of alternating nanoscale FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers.
The starting multilayer has severe lattice distortion and spatially variable short-range order.
The proposed intervention is constant sustained loading under isothermal, service-relevant creep conditions.
Creep will produce a spatially heterogeneous strain distribution concentrated near multilayer interfaces.
Dislocation pile-ups and interface-mediated slip will be concentrated near the multilayer interfaces.
Twinning may be localized near the multilayer interfaces during creep.
Conventional metallic multilayers and single-phase high-entropy alloys generally deform more uniformly under sustained loading.
Interface-mediated heterogeneous deformation dominates only when compositional complexity is pronounced and the nanoscale multilayer architecture remains intact.
Excessively thick layers or chemical simplification cause more uniform, traditional dislocation creep to prevail.
A lack of correlation between interfacial short-range-order variations and localized dislocation or twin activity, together with uniform deformation, would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
